analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal fuel economy standards for cars and light trucks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee after being referred in March 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed Title V of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act of 1975 — the law behind the CAFE program, which sets minimum average fuel economy (miles per gallon) that car and light truck makers must meet. It also would have let automakers use fuel economy credits they earned in past years to cover shortfalls in any year, with no time limit, removing the current three-year window. In effect, it would have ended the federal fuel economy mandate and erased a check on automakers that fall short. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Automakers, especially those selling larger, less efficient vehicles, would gain freedom from annual fuel economy targets and could bank old credits indefinitely instead of improving fleet mileage or paying penalties. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Automakers, especially truck and SUV sellers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Title V of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act of 1975, eliminating the fuel economy standards that apply to each automaker's fleet of cars and light trucks. [S2] [S3]
Lets manufacturers use CAFE credits earned before repeal to offset fuel economy deficits in any model year, removing the three-year limit on carrying credits forward and backward. [S2] [S3]
Makes the repeal retroactive, effective at the end of the 1989 model year and no later than December 31, 1989, even though the bill was introduced in 1993. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Drivers would bear higher fuel costs over time as new vehicles are allowed to burn more gasoline; the public also bears increased oil consumption and tailpipe emissions that fuel economy standards were designed to reduce.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drivers and the public, through fuel use

drawbacks.text: Repealing fuel economy standards would allow new cars and trucks to use more gasoline, raising what households spend at the pump compared with a world where the standards push mileage upward. [S2] [S3]
Eliminating the standards removes the main federal lever pushing automakers to improve efficiency, which means greater fuel consumption and emissions from the vehicle fleet. [S2]

The unlimited credit provision would let manufacturers cover shortfalls with decades-old credits indefinitely, weakening the penalty for missing the standard even in the years before repeal took full effect. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to one industry: automakers would escape compliance costs and penalties and gain flexibility to sell less efficient vehicles. The costs — higher gasoline spending for drivers and more fuel burned — fall on the public at large. The retroactive effective date and unlimited credit carry-forward make the relief for manufacturers broader still. There is no offsetting consumer or environmental benefit in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Carr introduced the bill on March 3, 1993. [S1] [S5]
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day. [S5]
On March 9, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, and no further action was taken. [S5]
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died in committee without reaching the floor. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, fuel economy standards for cars and light trucks stayed on the books, and drivers kept the lower fuel costs and reduced consumption the standards push toward. Automakers avoided getting the repeal they wanted, but also faced no vote or record on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drivers; the fuel standards stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Bob Carr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the CAFE fuel economy standards and allow unlimited use of fuel economy credits.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Energy and Power
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled consideration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 3, 1993, sent it to the Energy and Power subcommittee on March 9, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor from Michigan — an automaker state — no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the fuel economy standards automakers must meet and let them stretch old credits over any year without limit, cutting their compliance costs and penalties. Drivers would pay the difference in higher gasoline consumption. [S2] [S3]
Weaker fuel economy standards mean more gasoline burned per mile driven, increasing fuel sales. That cost lands on household budgets at the pump. [S2]
